The Best Countries World Cup: Groups E-H

Jay Biggerstaff|Getty Images

Kansas City Stadium stands ready ahead of the FIFA World World Cup 2026.

The 2026 World Cup is officially here, bringing an expanded field of 48 teams to North America to crown the undisputed champion of the soccer world. But while analysts are busy crunching expected goals and possession stats, we decided to look at a different kind of scoreboard. What if nations competed to see who was the best overall, rather than just the best on the pitch?

Relying on data from the U.S. News & World Report 2026 Best Countries rankings, we modeled what Best Countries matchups might look like among the nations competing in this year's tournament.

Yesterday we looked at Groups A through D. Here is how the data settles the score for Groups E, F, G, and H.

While Germany vs. Ecuador is expected to be one of the more interesting matches on the pitch, in a Best Countries matchup, it’s no contest. With high patent activity, R&D expenditure, and more high-tech exports than any country other than China, Germany ranks No. 3 in Economic Development. The European nation also ranks No. 4 in Culture & Tourism, No. 4 in Civic Health, No. 8 in Governance, and No. 4 overall.

While Ecuador does eke out one victory at the category level – ranking No. 20 in Natural Environment, compared to Germany at No. 27 – the South American nation ranks No. 82 overall. At the final whistle, Germany comfortably takes the three points, dominating across nearly every metric of national well-being.

One of the most fiercely competitive groups in this hypothetical Best Countries tournament is Group F. Japan takes on the Netherlands this weekend, pitting world-leading health outcomes against one of the most innovative liberal democracies on the planet. Japan’s life expectancy of 84 years is the second highest in the world, and the country ranks No. 5 in the Health category overall – well ahead of the Netherlands at No. 13. Japan also ranks No. 2 in Civic Health, aided by low homicide rates and high public trust.

Meanwhile, the Netherlands ranks No. 3 in Governance – due in part to low corruption perceptions, strong legal frameworks and the most UN treaty participation of any country other than the U.K. A deciding factor in this competitive game is in the Natural Environment category (Netherlands No. 17, Japan No. 82) where the Dutch pull ahead by virtue of sustainable, biodiversity-based trade and a high concentration of endemic native species. Ultimately, the Netherlands secures the win, ranking No. 5 overall, 12 spots above Japan at No. 17.

The marquee matchup of the group stage occurs the following weekend. Two top-tier, high-income European liberal democracies lock horns as Sweden faces the Netherlands, offering tight competition across nearly every category of national well-being. While in Economic Development the Netherlands (No. 8) beats Sweden (No. 13) due to greater market size and depth, Sweden outranks the Netherlands by several places in Health, Opportunity, Civic Health, and Culture & Tourism. Ultimately, Sweden ranks as the No. 3 best country overall, eking out a narrow victory over No. 5 Netherlands.

Group G contains one of the more competitive matchups between two highly developed nations as Belgium takes on New Zealand. The two countries are neck and neck in Governance (Belgium No. 14, New Zealand No. 13) and Opportunity (Belgium No. 12, New Zealand No. 13). While extensive conservation efforts and high air quality help New Zealand outclass Belgium in Natural Environment, the high-income European nation ultimately wins on Culture & Tourism, Economic Development, Health, Infrastructure and Civic Health. Belgium ranks No. 11 overall, comfortably above New Zealand at No. 21.

In another highly anticipated clash, Iran faces off against Egypt amid a backdrop defined by deep geopolitical friction and the ongoing Iran war. Egypt builds a lead with stronger performances in Natural Environment (Egypt No. 66, Iran No. 91) and Civic Health (Egypt No. 74, Iran No. 100). While Iran has slight edges in Health (No. 62 over Egypt's No. 87) and Opportunity (No. 83 over Egypt's No. 88), Egypt manages to secure the overall victory. Egypt ranks No. 80 in the 2026 Best Countries index, compared to Iran at No. 86.

While Spain is the group heavyweight and easily clears its rivals, Group H contains an interesting matchup in Saudi Arabia vs. Uruguay. The two countries show strong divergence at the subcategory level, yet rank similarly at the broader category level. Leading on factors like data skills, educational attainment and government expenditure on education, Saudi Arabia ranks No. 18 in Human Capital Development, versus Uruguay at No. 51. Meanwhile, low labor income relative to GDP and poor worker protections put Saudi Arabia at No. 71 in the Labor Market subcategory, far below Uruguay at No. 34. In the broader Opportunity subcategory, the two countries nearly tie (Saudi Arabia No. 47, Uruguay No. 46).

One of the largest contrasts comes in the Civic Health category. While Saudi Arabia – an absolute monarchy – ranks No. 96 in Human Rights & Freedoms, Uruguay leads the world at No. 1. Saudi Arabia wins a small victory in Public Safety, but the Middle Eastern economic power ranks No. 72 in Civic Health, far below Uruguay at No. 32. Overall, Uruguay claims a hard-fought victory, ranking No. 45 globally, while Saudi Arabia finishes a few spots behind at No. 51.

Whether it is a clash of high-income European democracies or a proxy battle reflecting deep geopolitical tensions, the World Cup has always been bigger than soccer. While the Best Countries index offers a powerful lens to analyze these rivalries, sometimes it is easier to settle international scores on the pitch. Enjoy the matches as they kick off this week, and keep an eye out for more of our upcoming group breakdowns.
